title: Why Is Marriage Under Attack Today?
paragraphs:
Why Is Marriage Under Attack Today?
The Battle Was Never Just About Romance—It Has Always Been About Destroying the Living Picture of Christ and His Church
There is a quiet question echoing through countless homes tonight.
Why does something God called very good seem to have become one of the hardest things to protect?

Why are marriages collapsing at record speed? Why do couples who once promised forever now struggle to survive another week? Why do loneliness, betrayal, pornography, selfishness, confusion, bitterness, emotional distance, financial pressure, and broken trust seem to surround marriage from every direction?
This is not merely a social problem.
It is a spiritual battle.
And if we misunderstand the battlefield, we will fight the wrong enemy.
Marriage is under attack today because it has always stood as one of God's greatest visible testimonies of His invisible Gospel.
The enemy has never simply hated weddings.
He hates what marriage reveals.
He hates what marriage preaches without words.
He hates the story marriage tells.
Because every faithful marriage whispers the greatest story ever told.
Jesus Christ loved His Bride.
He gave Himself for her.
He cleansed her.
He forgave her.
He redeemed her.
He will never abandon her.
That is why marriage matters.
Long before governments defined it...
Long before cultures debated it...
Long before traditions celebrated it...
Marriage belonged to God.
The opening chapters of Genesis introduce humanity with breathtaking simplicity.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew expression is דָּבַק (dāḇaq).
It means far more than simply "stay together."
It means to cling.
To adhere.
To remain firmly attached.
To pursue covenant loyalty.
This same Hebrew word is repeatedly used for Israel clinging faithfully to the LORD.
Marriage was never designed as temporary emotional chemistry.
It was covenant.
Not convenience.
God also says they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (bāśār ʾeḥād)—"one flesh."
This is far deeper than physical intimacy.
It speaks of an entirely new covenant union where two lives become one before God.
Marriage is not merely two people sharing a house.
It is two lives becoming one testimony.
Then sin entered.
Genesis 3 records humanity's rebellion.
Immediately, relationships fractured.
Shame appeared.
Blame followed.
Fear replaced intimacy.
Instead of Adam protecting Eve, he blamed her.
Instead of unity, division entered.
Marriage was not broken because God designed it poorly.
Marriage suffers because sin entered humanity.
The Bible never hides this reality.
Instead, it explains it.
Every marriage struggles because every heart struggles.
Jeremiah 17:9 reminds us:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
Notice where Scripture points.
Not first to politics.
Not first to entertainment.
Not first to society.
It begins with the human heart.
That is why no government can ultimately save marriage.
No law can create covenant love.
Only transformed hearts can.
Jesus Himself explained the root problem.
In Matthew 19, the Pharisees questioned Him about divorce.
Jesus answered by returning to Genesis.
He did not begin with legal loopholes.
He began with God's original design.
Then He declared:
"What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
The Greek phrase is ὃ οὖν ὁ Θεὸς συνέζευξεν (ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen).
The verb συνέζευξεν (synezeuxen) literally means "joined together under one yoke."
It pictures two lives intentionally fastened together by God Himself.
Marriage is not merely a contract.
It is divine joining.
That changes everything.
The modern world often teaches that love exists to satisfy personal happiness.
Scripture teaches that marriage exists to display God's covenant faithfulness.
Those are radically different foundations.
One asks:
"What can I receive?"
The other asks:
"How can I reflect Christ?"
The Apostle Paul reveals the mystery in Ephesians 5.
After instructing husbands and wives, he writes:
The Greek word for mystery is μυστήριον (mystērion).
Not something unknowable.
Something once hidden but now revealed.
Marriage was always pointing somewhere greater.
It points to Jesus.
Husbands are called to love "as Christ loved the church."
The Greek says:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν (kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen).
The verb ἠγάπησεν (ēgapēsen) comes from ἀγαπάω (agapaō)—self-giving covenant love.
Not emotional infatuation.
Not temporary attraction.
Sacrificial love.
Cross-shaped love.
Resurrection love.
Grace-filled love.
The world often celebrates romance.
Jesus demonstrates redemption.
That is why the cross transforms marriage more than flowers ever could.
Marriage is under attack because Satan has always sought to distort what reflects God's glory.
Jesus describes Satan in John 8:44 as "a liar and the father of lies."
His strategy has never changed.
If he cannot destroy God's image, he will distort it.
If he cannot stop the Gospel, he will attack the picture of the Gospel.
Marriage becomes one of his primary targets.
Today that attack appears through many different doors.
Self-centeredness replaces sacrificial love.
Entertainment replaces communication.
Pornography counterfeits intimacy.
Pride refuses forgiveness.
Bitterness hardens hearts.
Consumer culture treats spouses as disposable instead of covenant partners.
Even busyness quietly steals marriages.
Many couples no longer fight each other.
They simply stop seeing each other.
Two exhausted people become roommates instead of covenant companions.
Technology connects strangers while disconnecting families sitting at the same table.
None of these struggles surprise God.
Scripture anticipated the condition of fallen humanity.
Second Timothy 3 describes people becoming lovers of self rather than lovers of God.
When self becomes king, every relationship eventually suffers.
But the Gospel never leaves us in despair.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about damaged marriages.
It is about a Redeemer.
The greatest scandal in history was not simply humanity's rebellion.
It was that holy God willingly pursued guilty sinners anyway.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice the order.
Christ did not wait until His Bride became beautiful.
He died to make her beautiful.
He loved first.
He forgave first.
He pursued first.
This changes how Christian marriage works.
Forgiveness becomes possible because we have been forgiven.
Mercy becomes possible because mercy found us.
Grace becomes possible because grace rescued us.
Marriage becomes strongest not when two perfect people meet...
But when two forgiven sinners keep running back to the perfect Savior.
Perhaps your marriage is flourishing.
Praise God.
Guard it.
Pray over it.
Invest in it.
Do not assume healthy marriages remain healthy accidentally.
Perhaps your marriage feels exhausted.
Hope remains.
God still resurrects what people declare impossible.
Perhaps your marriage ended through tragedy, abandonment, or painful circumstances.
Hear this clearly.
Your identity is not your marital status.
Your identity is found in Christ.
The Gospel restores people before it restores relationships.
And sometimes God's deepest healing begins inside one surrendered heart.
Jesus has always specialized in rewriting impossible stories.
Peter denied Him.
David committed adultery.
Rahab carried a scandalous past.
The Samaritan woman had multiple broken relationships.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet every one of those stories encountered grace greater than failure.
This has always been God's way.
From scandal...
To grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Marriage is not ultimately protected by stronger emotions.
It is protected by deeper surrender.
The closer two people move toward Christ, the closer they inevitably move toward one another.
That is why revival inside homes has always begun with repentance before romance.
If this article stirred your heart, don't let it end here.

Which truth challenged you the most? If you need prayer for your marriage, your future marriage, or healing from a broken relationship, comment, "Pray for me." If Christ has been restoring your heart, comment, "Jesus is rewriting my story." Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else has been praying to see.
Your support enables us to continue producing Scripture-rich articles, devotionals, Gospel-centered resources, and messages that point people to Jesus rather than to personalities.
One faithful marriage may preach the Gospel more loudly than a thousand arguments ever could.
